strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed experiments across multiple models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and datasets with proper statistical reporting and controls
Valuable empirical insight that simpler adapters (scalar affine) generalize better than more expressive alternatives, with thorough ablation studies explaining why
Thoughtful mechanistic analysis using zero-vector interpretations (Appendix J) and ALL-CAPS experiments (Appendix I) to understand what adapters learn (bias as prior, input as semantics)

Practical utility: method is computationally cheap, preserves original model, and released code/adapters benefit community; works across diverse tasks (SAE labeling, topic identification, implicit reasoning)
Strong results on some metrics (94% vs 1% recall@1 on contrastive vectors, 91% vs 56% bridge entity detection) and demonstration of scaling benefits without model modification
Elegant core insight: reframing existing interpretability artifacts as training supervision for self-interpretation
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, comprehensive appendices enabling reproducibility, and good qualitative examples
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: training affine transformations on activation vectors is conceptually straightforward; concurrent work (Li et al., Karvonen et al.) explores related directions
Modest improvements in some settings (71% vs 63% generation scoring on SAE features at 70B; trained adapters underperform auto-interp on detection scoring 0.814 vs 0.821)
Generation scoring evaluation is indirect and unvalidated—no clear evidence it reliably measures semantic accuracy; best-of-6 protocol complicates comparisons despite fairness

Incomplete mechanistic understanding of key phenomena: cross-layer generalization explanation is speculative; intrinsic dimensionality hypothesis supported but not definitive; limited failure mode analysis
Evaluation limitations: bridge entity detection on only 500 examples from one dataset; unclear if scaling trends hold beyond 72B; only tangential comparison to concurrent fine-tuning approaches
Limited scope: approach works well for monosemantic vectors by construction; generalization to truly polysemantic residual streams shown empirically but not theoretically motivated
Presentation could be more concise (23 pages); key mechanistic insights relegated to appendices; some architectural choices (e.g., layer 19) appear arbitrary and unjustified

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), datasets (Goodfire, Llama Scope, Wikipedia), and metrics (generation scoring, detection scoring, retrieval)
Thoughtful ablation studies and controlled experiments that isolate dimensionality as the critical factor explaining full-rank vs. scalar affine performance differences
Honest discussion of limitations: acknowledges that scale sensitivity persists, data dependence is severe, and architecture must be selected per data type
Valuable mechanistic insights showing bias vector encodes 'default interpretation prior' while input vector specifies semantics, with clear zero-vector experiments
Extensive reproducibility support including detailed hyperparameters, experimental protocols, and promised code release
weaknesses: Scale sensitivity not genuinely solved: method still requires best-of-6 grid search at inference; Figure 4 shows trained adapters simply have broader valid ranges rather than eliminating the problem

Severe data dependence undermines generality: Wikipedia-trained adapters achieve only 49.7% hit rate on Goodfire SAEs (vs. 62.8% for Goodfire-trained); cross-dataset transfer is weak, requiring task-specific training for each application

Inconsistent architecture across data types: full-rank works for low-intrinsic-dimensionality topics but fails catastrophically on SAEs; this ad-hoc design requirement based on unknown data properties is inelegant

Questionable evaluation methodology: generation scoring is somewhat circular (testing model consistency on synthetic contexts); detection scoring (standard SAE metric) shows trained adapters underperform auto-interp labels (0.774-0.814 vs. 0.821 F1), contradicting other metrics

Limited technical novelty: training supervised mappings is standard ML; Patchscopes framework is prior work; unsurprising finding that simpler models generalize better in high-dimensional spaces; concurrent fine-tuning work not empirically compared

Bridge entity detection application limited to 12% of dataset (5,546 filtered to 500 questions) with stark training-data dependence: Wikipedia-trained achieves 91% vs. SAE-trained 66.4%, suggesting task-specific fit rather than general capability

Modest improvements despite data requirements: Table 2 shows 4.5 percentage point gains over paraphrases; Table 3 shows 8 point gain at 70B—solid but not transformative given need for task-specific training

Missing key comparisons: no empirical comparison with concurrent Li et al. (2025) fine-tuning approaches; claims about frozen models preserving 'privileged access' are not validated against alternatives

strengths: Elegant approach with strong empirical results: achieves 71% SAE label accuracy (70B) vs 49% untrained and 94% recall@1 on topic identification, demonstrating clear practical improvements

Rigorous experimental design with multiple evaluation metrics (generation scoring, detection scoring, embedding-based retrieval), fair best-of-6 protocol applied consistently to baselines, and extensive ablations across data shuffling, training data scaling, and architecture variants

Novel insights into adapter behavior: discovery that bias vector accounts for ~85% of improvement is surprising and well-demonstrated; clear analysis of identity-preserving structure's importance and intrinsic dimensionality hypothesis

Strong scaling analysis with Taboo baseline effectively isolates self-interpretation gains from capability gains; demonstrates SelfIE performance improves faster than model knowledge saturation with scale

Comprehensive experimental scope: multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), multiple datasets (SAE features, contrastive vectors, bridge entity detection), cross-layer and cross-dataset generalization studies
Practical utility: computationally efficient (~10 GPU-hours at 70B), leverages existing interpretability artifacts, frozen model approach valuable for alignment, code/adapter release promised

Exceptional documentation: 23-page appendix with detailed protocols, hyperparameters, dataset creation procedures, ablations, and reproducibility guidance; informative figures particularly Figure 2 with Taboo baseline
weaknesses: Best-of-6 protocol design choice: while fairly applied, selecting best among 6 scales is somewhat artificial; Figure 4 shows trained adapters work at more scales but doesn't establish uniform performance across scales vs baseline's peak at single scale

Claims about outperforming training labels need qualification: '71% vs 63%' framing compares trained adapter to paraphrased labels rather than best baseline; original labels (54.8%) are much lower, making improvement appear larger than 71-63 gap

Generation scoring metric somewhat circular: success depends on model's capability to generate appropriate feature examples; detection scoring on pre-compiled activations is more objective, though Appendix Table 2 provides F1 scores as independent validation
Limited empirical engagement with concurrent work (Li et al. 2025; Karvonen et al. 2025): claims about frozen model advantages over fine-tuning lack head-to-head comparisons despite conceptual appeal

Bridge entity detection (Section 3.5) tangential to main narrative: claims about 'what the model is thinking' are interpretive rather than demonstrative; alignment heuristic for position 0 could introduce subtle biases

Incomplete analysis of cross-dataset generalization: SAE-trained adapter underperforms Wikipedia-trained (66% vs 91% bridge entity detection) with post-hoc explanation; Table 2 patterns complex but underexplored

Limited scope: only instruction-tuned models, requires existing interpretability artifacts or contrastive vector computation, performance varies significantly across datasets (GemmaScope 42.5% vs Goodfire 49.7%), 32B scaling anomaly (Figure 15) lacks convincing explanation

Potential overclaiming: 'implicit reasoning' and 'catching models red-handed' framing in Section 3.5 may overstate what's demonstrated; improvements don't guarantee truthfulness or prevent deceptive alignment

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen), scales (7B-72B), and datasets with rigorous statistical reporting including SEM and proper train/val/test separation
Sophisticated two-phase scoring protocol to avoid selection-on-noise bias and clear separation of candidate selection from final evaluation, demonstrating methodological care

Insightful analysis of why architecture choice matters: intrinsic dimensionality analysis (PCA) explains full-rank overfitting on high-dimensional SAE space but not low-dimensional Wikipedia vectors, with controlled experiments isolating this factor

Novel insights into adapter function: bias vector as 'interpretation prior' demonstrated through ALL-CAPS training experiment and zero-vector interpretations, showing clean decomposition of bias vs. input contributions
Key practical finding that scalar affine adapters with only d_model+1 parameters achieve 85% of gains from best model, with excellent generalization across datasets compared to complex alternatives
Proper experimental controls including Taboo baseline for scaling analysis that isolates self-interpretation gains from general capability improvements
Freezes original model weights, preserving behavior and privileged access unlike fine-tuning approaches; enables adapters to improve with model scale without modifying interpretations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: training adapters on existing vector-label pairs is a straightforward baseline; core contribution is empirical rather than methodological, and framing as 'solving hyperparameter sensitivity' overstates the advance

Circular evaluation claim: adapters trained on noisy auto-interpretability labels outperforming those labels is expected regression behavior (averaging smooths noise), not genuine breakthrough; lacks human evaluation validating improvements are meaningful

Critical fundamental limitation: method requires pre-existing interpretability artifacts (SAE labels or synthetic descriptions), limiting applicability to new models/layers and creating circular dependency on expensive SAE training

Scale selection hyperparameter favorably calibrates trained adapters using validation set; 'best-of-N' with N=6 performs implicit hyperparameter search not fairly compared against fixed baselines, and different scales optimize different metrics (detection vs. generation)

Poor cross-dataset generalization contradicts claims: Wikipedia→SAE transfer shows 8.7% vs 47% performance (57% gap); SAE→Wikipedia transfer <3.5%, indicating methods are dataset-specific rather than robust

Insufficient alternative comparisons: LoRA shows comparable performance (81.6% vs 82.9% on Wikipedia); linear probes only compared on bridge task; no comparison with other recent adapter methods; Tuned Lens comparison purely qualitative

Detection vs. generation metric disagreement (Appendix K) reveals systematic divergence in which labels selected per latent, suggesting metrics measure different notions of 'correct' interpretation; paper lacks discussion of implications

Bridge entity detection experiment is artificial: filtered only to cases where model gives correct immediate answers, limited to 500 questions, and SAE-trained adapters perform worse than Wikipedia-trained (66% vs 91%), contradicting claims about monosemantic→polysemantic transfer

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and diverse representation types (SAEs, contrastive vectors), demonstrating broad applicability
Well-designed experimental methodology with proper safeguards against selection bias (two-phase scoring protocol in Appendix A.5), held-out evaluation, and extensive ablations

Surprising and useful empirical finding that simpler scalar affine adapters generalize better than higher-capacity alternatives, traced mechanistically to intrinsic dimensionality differences (Appendix D)
Thorough analysis of what adapters learn: the bias vector acts as an interpretation prior (85% of improvement), with clear decomposition shown via ALL-CAPS experiments (Appendix I)
Practical contribution: extremely lightweight adapters (d+1 parameters) are computationally cheap to train (~10 GPU-hours at 70B) and improve interpretation reliability across model scales
Excellent reproducibility: extensive appendices with hyperparameters, dataset details, training procedures, and proper statistical reporting with standard errors and significance tests
Novel application showing adapters trained on monosemantic vectors transfer to arbitrary activations in multi-hop reasoning (Section 3.6), with 91% vs 56% bridge entity detection
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is applying standard lightweight adapters to learned transformations—a straightforward engineering solution rather than a fundamental advance in understanding model internals

Evaluation heavily relies on automatic metrics (generation/detection scoring, embedding-based retrieval) that may not capture true interpretation quality; no human evaluation of whether generated descriptions are actually useful or meaningful

Circular dependency on interpretability artifacts: training and evaluating on SAE/contrastive features assumes these artifacts are correct. The paper doesn't validate whether the approach reveals anything new about model representations beyond what SAEs/contrastive methods already capture

Metric disagreement undermines confidence: detection and generation scoring select different labels at opposite ends of scale grid (Appendix K), suggesting the metrics are measuring fundamentally different properties rather than converging on label quality

Comparable or inferior performance vs. concurrent work (Karvonen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025): LoRA achieves 81.6% vs 82.9% recall@1 on Wikipedia, and unlike fine-tuning approaches, adapters cannot answer arbitrary natural language queries about activations

Bridge entity detection evaluation (Section 3.6) limited to 12% of TwoHopFact dataset where models answer immediately without CoT; generalization to other implicit reasoning tasks unclear, and improvements are on a narrow filtered subset
Scale selection procedure (logarithmic grid calibrated on small subset) lacks robustness analysis; sensitivity to this hyperparameter choice not discussed, yet it significantly affects performance

Incomplete comparisons: no ablation comparing empirical scale-tuning for each vector (simpler baseline) vs. learning an adapter; linear probe comparison only on bridge entity detection, not main tasks

Training on noisy auto-interpretability labels: improvements might partly reflect denoising/ensembling multiple noisy SAE labels rather than true interpretation ability, confounding the interpretation of results

strengths: Rigorous experimental methodology with two-phase protocol to eliminate selection-on-noise bias; comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and metrics with proper statistical reporting
Surprising and well-supported findings about adapter scaling benefits and the surprising importance of the bias vector (~85% of improvement from d-dimensional bias alone)
Insightful architectural analysis explaining why full-rank adapters overfit on high-dimensional SAE data but not low-dimensional Wikipedia vectors, with controlled experiments isolating confounds
Exceptional reproducibility documentation including detailed hyperparameters, training protocols, evaluation procedures, and transparent computational costs (~180-220 GPU-hours total)
Consistent improvements across model families (Llama, Gemma, Qwen) and diverse evaluation metrics (generation scoring, detection F1, embedding retrieval) demonstrating robustness

Clever decomposition of adapter function through ALL-CAPS experiments and zero-vector interpretations revealing that bias encodes a 'prior' distribution while input vector provides semantic specificity
Practical value: lightweight, frozen-model approach trains efficiently and keeps base model unchanged; leverages existing interpretability artifacts as training signal
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: learning affine transformations is straightforward; application to self-interpretation is practical but incremental without significant new theoretical insights

Fundamental evaluation ambiguity: detection and generation scoring metrics substantially disagree (Table 2, Appendix K); adapters match auto-interp baseline on detection (0.722 F1) but only outperform on generation (47.6% vs 41.1%), making 'outperforms training labels' claim metric-dependent and potentially misleading

Poor cross-dataset generalization: Wikipedia-trained adapters achieve only 8.7% R@1 on SAE features; SAE-trained adapters degrade to 66.4% bridge entity detection (vs. 91% for Wikipedia-trained), with no principled way to predict transfer success

Training data dependency: method requires pre-existing labeled vector datasets; performance heavily depends on training label quality, which is not systematically studied; unclear how to apply to novel emergent behaviors

Scale selection still required: contrary to claims about removing hyperparameter sensitivity, method uses a 12-value scale grid and best-of-N selection at inference, only reducing (not eliminating) sensitivity

Generation scoring methodology concerns: indirect measurement requiring synthetic example generation and checking activations; binary hit/miss metric doesn't capture activation magnitude; limited analysis of failure modes

Incomplete baseline comparisons: LoRA fine-tuning relegated to brief mention showing comparable performance; limited comparison with other activation interpretation methods; main baseline (untrained SelfIE) is known to be brittle
Bridge entity detection results are modest: 91% detection rate but only 4.26%±0.24 of generations contain the bridge entity; practical utility unclear given low generation frequency

Missing ablations: no systematic study of training data size effects beyond Figure 7, adapter initialization sensitivity, optimal injection layer, or training on detection-optimal vs. generation-optimal labels separately

Incomplete conceptual analysis: limited discussion of when adapters can be trusted or produce plausible false descriptions; 'privileged access hypothesis' mentioned but not tested; no adversarial robustness analysis; unclear how improved descriptions actually help alignment/safety applications
